transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-03-21
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Anya Kovács (Silverpine Head of Security), Marc Ruiz (Silverpine Platform Eng), Sofie Lund (Silverpine Counsel)

Summary:
Quick security and compliance review focused on Silverpine's requirement for strict EU-only processing of customer data, bring-your-own-key (BYOK) KMS options, and what contractual and technical controls Redwood can provide to guarantee region pinning and auditability. Action items agreed to share artifacts and run a short benchmark.

Topics covered:
- EU-only region pin / hard region locking
- KMS BYOK vs Redwood-managed keys, HSM custody, and escrow
- Subprocessor list (EU footprint) and contractual limitations
- RBAC / SSO / audit log retention and access for compliance + e-discovery
- SOC 2 / ISO artifacts and audit cadence
- Fallback behavior and detectable cross-border exceptions

Action items (brief):
- Redwood: send subprocessor list + SOC2/ISO docs
- SE: run latency checks from Frankfurt VPC and document KMS flow
- Legal: exchange DPA redline for region-locking clause

Transcript (timestamps approximate, transcription imperfect in places):
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Anya Kovács: Hi, Anya here. Head of Sec at Silverpine.
[00:08] Marc Ruiz: Marc, platform.
[00:10] Sofie Lund: Sofie from legal.
[00:12] Liam O'Connor: Liam, SE at Redwood.
[00:14] Maya Chen: Great. Today we're circling on EU-only processing and KMS options, and to align on deliverables. Anya, can you kick us off with the high level of the requirement?
[00:25] Anya Kovács: Sure. We have a regulatory constraint for a subset of PII and genomic-derived outputs that must never leave EU jurisdiction. Our product owners want a hard region pin - not just preference - so, like, all inference, logging, and derived artifacts stay within EU. No cross-border transit except some admin meta maybe. We also require customer-managed keys where possible, so BYOK is preferred.
[00:49] Maya Chen: Got it. When you say hard pin, do you mean contractual requirement plus technical enforcement?
[00:53] Anya Kovács: Yes, both. Contract plus proof in logs and attestations. We need to be able to demonstrate to auditors that processing never occurred outside EU for those datasets.
[01:05] Liam O'Connor: Okay, we have two mechanisms generally: region affinity with strict routing + dedicated private deployments. For hosted customers we do region pinning at the VPC edge and also maintain a private control plane option for Private deployments. I should flag that if you want hosted with hard legal guarantees, we typically pair it with a Dedicated or Private deployment model.
[01:28] Marc Ruiz: So dedicated capacity in EU only, right? What about fallbacks - if capacity saturates, will requests go to the US?
[01:36] Liam O'Connor: By default we won't fail open to US for region-pinned orgs. There's a configuration policy: hard-lock mode will reject requests if EU capacity isn't available. There's also a soft-fallback mode that will route to nearby compatible region with alerts. For strict compliance you want hard-lock.
[01:51] Marc Ruiz: Good, reject is fine but we need clear SLA around availability.
[01:56] Maya Chen: We'll include dedicated capacity SLOs and fail/reject semantics in the DPA/SLA.
[02:02] Sofie Lund: On KMS, we need BYOK with customer key custody - ideally hardware-backed keys. How do you handle key material and HSM custody?
[02:12] Liam O'Connor: We support two BYOK flows: 1) customer uploads key material to our KMS provider with a customer-managed envelope key and Redwood never sees plaintext (managed KMS), 2) or you run an external HSM and use an API token for encryption-at-rest - that's the most strict. For escrow, we can offer a key-escrow process with limited access in case of emergency but that's usually tightly controlled and contracted.
[02:33] Anya Kovács: Is the key material ever visible to subprocessors in the chain, e.g., if compute is on partner infra?
[02:38] Liam O'Connor: No. With BYOK the envelope key is stored with your KMS. Our compute nodes only receive encrypted model artifacts and encrypted KV caches; all decryption is done in the compute environment using the ephemeral key provided at runtime. We can provide a decryption flow diagram.
[02:53] Marc Ruiz: Can you confirm HSM providers in EU? We have a preference for HSMs hosted in FR/DE.
[02:58] Maya Chen: We support major KMS/HSM providers in EU—KeyVault-EU, CloudHSM-EU, and partners. We'll send a canonical list.
[03:06] Sofie Lund: We'll want the subprocessor list constrained to EU data centers only, or at least called out which subprocessors may process metadata in the US.
[03:14] Liam O'Connor: We'll export the subprocessor inventory filtered by region and role. For EU-only commitments we can contractually exclude any non-EU subprocessors from handling that specific dataset.
[03:24] Anya Kovács: Auditability: we need immutable audit logs and the ability to export them for e-discovery. Retention: 7 years for certain events. Can you support that?
[03:34] Liam O'Connor: Yes, we persist audit logs with configurable retention up to multi-year. Logs are write-once in an append-only store with integrity checks. We can provide certified log export (signed) and chain-of-custody reports.
[03:46] Marc Ruiz: How about RBAC and SSO? We need role separation so platform engineers don't see customer secrets.
[03:52] Maya Chen: We integrate with SAML SSO and SCIM for provisioning. RBAC is fine-grained: project, model, and key-level roles. We can mirror your internal groups and we support just-in-time admin elevation with audit trails.
[04:06] Anya Kovács: Perfect. One area we worry about is inadvertent cross-border caching—like KV cache being replicated for efficiency.
[04:13] Liam O'Connor: Good callout. For region-locked tenants we disable cross-region KV cache replication and partition caches to the EU region only. I'll note that the transcript may show KV "cash" in earlier notes, but we mean KV cache.
[04:26] (laughter)
[04:28] Sofie Lund: From a legal perspective we'll want guaranteed data residency plus audit rights, plus a defined incident notification window for cross-border leaks.
[04:37] Maya Chen: Our standard incident SLA is 72 hours for P1, but for region-binding customers we can negotiate a shorter window. We also have mandatory notification if any region exception is triggered.
[04:48] Marc Ruiz: On the technical side, will Redwood's model selection or fallbacks ever cause data to leave EU? For example, if a lower-latency model is only hosted in US, would that be used?
[04:58] Liam O'Connor: No, not for hard-locked workloads. We have model variants and we can pin model versions in EU-only pools. The runtime will not route to US-hosted models if the tenant is region-locked.
[05:09] Anya Kovács: Good. Another ask: can we see evidence of SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 scans specifically for EU regions, not just global statements?
[05:18] Maya Chen: We'll include regional evidence where possible; our SOC2 covers the control plane and regional operational practices and we can provide auditor letters.
[05:26] Sofie Lund: About subcontractors—if Redwood uses a CDN or logging provider in the US for non-sensitive telemetry, is that allowed? We need an explicit mapping of what can touch US infra.
[05:36] Liam O'Connor: We'll provide a mapping. Typically non-sensitive operational telemetry can be aggregated in other regions, but for your constrained dataset we can mark everything PII-sensitive to remain in EU and route telemetry to EU-only collectors.
[05:50] Marc Ruiz: Latency question — can we get an example token latency from our Frankfurt VPC to your EU-dedicated pool?
[05:57] Liam O'Connor: Yes. We'll run a simple test: 1k sample requests, typical prompt size 60 tokens. Expected p95 token latency in EU dedicated pool around 30-60ms depending on model. We'll share the raw numbers.
[06:11] Anya Kovács: Can you talk through encryption in transit and at rest? We require TLS 1.3 for transit and AES-256 for at-rest.
[06:19] Maya Chen: We enforce TLS1.3 across endpoints. At rest we use KMS-backed AES-256 with customer-managed envelope keys where BYOK is enabled.
[06:28] Sofie Lund: A curious point — how do you prove no inadvertent snapshots or backups are stored outside EU? Backups sometimes go to centralized storage.
[06:36] Liam O'Connor: For EU-pinned workloads we use EU-only storage buckets and disable global backup replication. We'll provide S3-like bucket policies and retention configuration examples.
[06:47] Marc Ruiz: Do you support log exports to our SIEM in EU? We use an on-prem SIEM in DE.
[06:52] Liam O'Connor: Yes, we can push signed log exports to your SIEM endpoint in DE via secure transfer, or you can pull them via a signed API. We support syslog over TLS and SFTP drop with signed manifests.
[07:06] Anya Kovács: For audit we also need to be able to run discovery queries — e-discovery — on the logs.
[07:11] Liam O'Connor: We provide search/export tools with RBAC-limited access and can schedule periodic exports to your e-discovery pipeline.
[07:20] Sofie Lund: On subprocessors, can you confirm whether any third-party managed services—like a metrics aggregator—are located outside EU and might see metadata?
[07:29] Maya Chen: We'll produce a subprocessor spreadsheet filtered by function and region. For strict EU-only contracts we can exclude particular non-EU processors for that dataset.
[07:38] Marc Ruiz: Are there any additional certifications for EU infrastructure?
[07:41] Liam O'Connor: Many of our partners hold ISO 27001 and we have region-specific attestations. We'll include certification details in the packet.
[07:50] Anya Kovács: A scenario: emergency access required by Redwood engineering to fix a production issue — how is that controlled and logged?
[07:59] Liam O'Connor: Emergency access is controlled by break-glass with approval workflow, time-limited keys, and full session recording. All break-glass events generate an immutable audit entry and we can produce custody logs.
[08:13] Sofie Lund: We'll want the DPA to enumerate those emergency access conditions and who may approve them.
[08:19] Maya Chen: Agreed. We'll propose language and share examples of break-glass workflows.
[08:25] Marc Ruiz: Any performance tradeoffs with BYOK or HSM?
[08:29] Liam O'Connor: Minimal. Envelope key operations happen at session start; per-token overhead is negligible. HSM lookups might add a few milliseconds to session init.
[08:38] Anya Kovács: One more question: can you prove data locality for a given inference request, like a signed attestation that shows the request was processed in FR?
[08:47] Liam O'Connor: Yes — we can generate signed processing attestations that include the region, node id, and timestamp. Those are signed with our attestation key and you can verify them back to our cert chain.
[08:58] Sofie Lund: We'll want the attestation flow documented. Also, retention of attestation records aligned with log retention.
[09:06] Maya Chen: We'll include attestation docs and retention policy mapping.
[09:12] (Short pause)
[09:15] Marcus (background): [unintelligible]
[09:18] Liam O'Connor: A couple of slightly messy bits in the notes — earlier we mentioned model fallbacks. To be extra explicit: for EU-hard locked accounts, the routing table for that tenant only contains EU pools. No US endpoints are allowed.
[09:33] Marc Ruiz: Ok that resolves the model fallback concern.
[09:36] Anya Kovács: On the legal side, we'll have a few edits around contractual audit rights and the remedies for inadvertent cross-border processing.
[09:44] Sofie Lund: Also, can Redwood accept EU-focused data residency clauses that include audit windows and sample audits?
[09:51] Maya Chen: Yes, we accept sample audits under NDA and can support remote inspection plus the occasional on-site audit for enterprise Private deployments.
[09:59] Marc Ruiz: For testing, we'll want a short pilot in EU to validate the flows. What's the minimal pilot configuration?
[10:06] Liam O'Connor: Typically a small dedicated pool (1-2 GPUs) pinned to EU with BYOK and sample traffic works. We'll also wire SIEM exports and run the latency tests. That should be enough to validate residency, KMS flow, and logs.
[10:20] Anya Kovács: How long to spin up a pilot?
[10:22] Maya Chen: With Dedicated provisioning, about 48-72 hours for setup and key onboarding if everything is pre-approved.
[10:29] Sofie Lund: On data subject requests — we need the ability to remove records and purge derived artifacts for EU subjects. Is there a purge API?
[10:37] Liam O'Connor: Yes, we have a data deletion API with a verifiable purge token and we maintain purge logs. For model-derived artifacts we also have a revocation flow for indexed outputs.
[10:49] Marc Ruiz: Will deletion propagate to backups?
[10:52] Liam O'Connor: For EU-only we set backup retention windows and can run targeted scrubs; there's a documented process for removing items from backups and we produce a removal certificate.
[11:03] Anya Kovács: That should cover regulatory expectations.
[11:06] (brief cross-talk)
[11:10] Maya Chen: Okay, recap and next steps: Redwood will send subprocessor list and SOC2/ISO evidence by Friday 2028-03-24; Liam will run the Frankfurt latency and BYOK verification by 2028-03-27; Sofie and Redwood legal will exchange DPA redlines by 2028-03-30. Also, we'll propose an initial pilot plan (1-2 GPU pool) and estimated provisioning times.
[11:36] Sofie Lund: That works. Please include the attestation examples and the break-glass workflow in the packet.
[11:42] Maya Chen: Will do. Anything else?
[11:45] Marc Ruiz: None from me.
[11:46] Anya Kovács: Nothing. Thanks.
[11:48] Maya Chen: Thanks all, we'll follow up in email. Bye.

End of transcript.
